sentences.text: Cyamodus possessed an armored carapace made of irregular hexagonal plates and large rounded teeth adapted for crushing hard-shelled prey.
The animal had a turtle-like flat body with a two-part carapace on its upper surface.
Its skull was heart-shaped and broad.
Cyamodus lacked dorsal spines but possessed a wing-like, elongated, flattened lateral spine that braced the subdermal carapace.
Most species measured between 1.3 and 1.5 meters in length and weighed 20 to 25 kilograms.
Fossil evidence of two juveniles inside a Lariosaurus stomach suggests the species was vulnerable to predation.
The genus was described by Christian Erich Hermann von Meyer in 1863 based on fossils found in Germany.
The first remains were discovered in Upper Muschelkalk shallow marine limestones near Bayreuth in Bavaria, Germany.
A complete skeleton of C. hildegardis was found in Switzerland outside the Germanic Basin in the northern Tethys.
The only known complete skeleton, including the skull, is that of C. hildegardis, found outside the German Basin in the northern Tethys Sea in present-day Switzerland.
Six species of Cyamodus have been identified: C. rostratus, C. munsteri, C. tarnowitzensis, C. hildegardis, C. kuhnschneyderi, and C. orientalis.
Cyamodus was a heavily armored swimmer specialized in uprooting and crushing shellfish with its powerful jaws.
Cyamodus likely lived by foraging on the sea floor, sucking up shellfish, and crushing them with its blunt teeth.
Cyamodus was more agile than other single-shelled placodonts like Henodus, despite its cumbersome shell.
The hexagonal plates on Cyamodus's shell increased protection and weight, an adaptation that helped it dive to reach shellfish.
Cyamodus was initially thought to be an ancestral turtle but was later reclassified as a placodont related to other Triassic turtle-like reptiles.
Cyamodus belongs to the order Placodontia, suborder Sauropterygia, superfamily Cyamodontoidea, and family Cyamodontidae.
Cyamodus is classified in the class Reptilia.
The type species of the genus Cyamodus is Cyamodus muensteri.
Fossils of Cyamodus date from the Middle Triassic, specifically from the Anisian to Ladinian stages.

While C.G. Diedrich suggested Cyamodus was an algae-grazer, this view is widely rejected by researchers like Torsten M. Scheyer, and the consensus remains that placodonts (except Henodus) were durophagous.
An intriguing placodont described by Giovanni Pinna in 1990, Protenodontosaurus italicus, appears to be intermediate between Cyamodus and the placocheilids.
